implementation_notes: Rust makes the snapshot explicit rather than automatic: derive Clone on the state type and the memento is a cloned value, held in a Vec<State> (or a VecDeque with a fixed capacity) that plays the caretaker, with restore as an assignment. Clone is documented as always producing a new value but not necessarily a deep one - Arc, Rc and other smart pointers clone the pointer and share the pointee - so state built from Arc<Mutex<T>> or Rc<RefCell<T>> snapshots the handle, not the contents. Because the borrow checker forbids holding references into a state you are about to mutate, undo stacks own their snapshots; persistent data structures (for example the im crate) are the escape hatch when cloning whole states is too expensive.
pitfalls: Deriving Clone on a struct that contains Arc<Mutex<T>> shares the mutable state with the snapshot, as the standard library documentation warns - the clone is a handle copy, not a state copy.
Borrows cannot be stored across mutations: a snapshot must own its data, so cheap snapshots require Rc/Arc or persistent structures, with the aliasing caveats above.
A Vec history grows without bound and keeps every cloned state alive; drain or cap it explicitly.
Clone has no deep-copy contract for smart pointers, and Copy is only for trivially copyable types; a type with a hand-written Clone must actually copy what it claims to.

variants.name: serde-serialized mementos (JSON/postcard)
variants.implementation_notes: When snapshots must be persisted or exchanged, derive Serialize/Deserialize and let serde encode the state to a data format: serde_json for readable history, postcard or bincode for compact binary checkpoints. serde is built on traits rather than runtime reflection, so the derive generates the code at compile time and serialization stays close to hand-written speed; the round-trip produces a fully independent value, which also serves as an explicit deep copy for state whose Clone is only a handle copy. Use it for durable history, undo across restarts, or when the memento must be validated by a schema before it is applied.
pitfalls: Deserialization trusts the input shape: a snapshot from an older or hostile source can fail or silently drop fields, so version the payload (serde defaults, tagged enums) and validate before restoring.
Formats are not interchangeable - JSON loses Rust-specific types (u64 beyond 2^53 in JavaScript, NaN) that binary formats preserve, so pick the format with the fidelity the state needs.
Serializing on every change costs allocations and encoding time; reserve it for checkpoints or persistence boundaries.
